unit.title: Troubleshoot and repair basic electrical/electronic apparatus

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Mrs Campbell brings in a fan that will not start. What should you do first?
options: Take it apart at once to look inside
Plug it in and shake it to see if it starts
Order a new motor for it straight away
Ask her what happened and how it fails

questions.stem: What is the usual order of work for finding a fault?
options: Replace parts one by one until it works, then test it
Collect information, inspect, test, then repair
Repair first, then ask what was wrong
Test it live, then look for damage

questions.stem: What is the first check to make on a faulty appliance after it is unplugged?
options: A visual check of the cord, plug and case
An insulation test at 1000 V
A run test on full load
A voltage test at the switch

questions.stem: Before you open a faulty kettle to test it, what must you do?
options: Fill it with water to keep it cool
Switch it off at its own switch only
Unplug it and keep the plug in view
Wear rubber gloves and leave it plugged in

questions.stem: Why must a resistance (ohms) test be made only on a circuit with no power?
options: The meter battery would go flat
The meter could be damaged and the reading wrong
The circuit would use less power
The resistance of the circuit would get much higher

questions.stem: You have just measured current with a multimeter. What must you do before you measure voltage?
options: Change the meter battery
Zero the meter on its ohms range first
Turn the meter over and tap it on the bench
Move the lead back to the voltage socket

questions.stem: How do you check a power cord for a broken conductor?
options: Test each conductor end to end for continuity
Measure the voltage across the plug pins with a meter
Bend it back and forth while it is plugged in
Look at the colour of the cord

questions.stem: A 1100 W kettle element works on 110 V. About what resistance should it read?
The element of a toaster reads infinite (open circuit) on the ohms range. What is the fault?
options: The element is working normally
The element is shorted to the case
The thermostat is set too high
The element wire is broken

questions.stem: What does a thermal fuse in an iron or kettle do?
options: Opens the circuit for good if it gets too hot
Turns the heat up and down to the setting chosen
Lights up to show the power is on
Stops the cord from being pulled out

questions.stem: A thermal fuse has blown. What should you replace it with?
options: A piece of copper wire
Any fuse that fits the same space in the appliance
One of the same type and temperature rating
A thermostat from another appliance

questions.stem: After you replace a blown thermal fuse, why should you find out why it blew?
options: So that you can charge the customer much more for it
So the new one does not blow for the same reason
So you can write a longer report
Because fuses never blow by themselves

questions.stem: What is the job of the thermostat in an electric iron?
options: To protect against shock
To light the power lamp
To cut the power if it is dropped
To keep the heat at the set level

questions.stem: How do you test an appliance switch with the appliance unplugged?
options: Check continuity with the switch ON and OFF
Measure the voltage across it
Press it many times quickly and listen to the click
Look at the colour of the switch

questions.stem: Why is the continuity from the metal case to the plug's earth pin tested after a repair?
options: To check the metal case is painted well
So a fault to the case trips the supply
To find the power rating of the appliance
To check that the on/off switch works

questions.stem: Which test after a repair shows there is no leakage path from the live parts to the metal case?
options: A continuity test of the cord
A polarity test of the plug
An insulation resistance test
A voltage test at the switch

questions.stem: On a two-pin polarised plug, which blade is the wider one?
options: The neutral blade
The line (live) blade
The earth blade
Both are the same

questions.stem: When you replace a faulty part, what should the new part match?
options: Its colour and its shape only
The cheapest part in the shop
Any part that fits the space
The same type, rating and size

questions.stem: What is the "half-split" method of fault finding?
options: Cutting the faulty cable in half
Testing at the middle, then in the bad half
Asking two different people to look for the fault
Replacing half of the parts at a time

questions.stem: A resistor has colour bands brown, black, red. What is its value?
How do you test a resistor you think is faulty on a circuit board?
options: Measure it with one leg lifted out
Measure the current through it with the power on
Heat it with the soldering iron
Bend its legs to see if it breaks

questions.stem: When a good diode is tested with a meter's diode test, what should you see?
options: A reading both ways
No reading in either direction
Zero ohms both ways
A reading one way only

questions.stem: Why must an electrolytic capacitor be fitted the right way round?
options: It looks neater on the board
It can be damaged or burst if reversed
It will make the circuit run faster
It changes the values of the resistors near it

questions.stem: Why must large capacitors in a power supply be discharged before you work on it?
options: They make the board too heavy
They will slow down the soldering iron when hot
They can store a charge after unplugging
They switch the power back on

questions.stem: What should a good soldered joint look like?
options: Smooth and shiny, and well flowed
A large ball of solder sitting on top
Dull, grey and cracked
Solder joining it to the next joint

questions.stem: What is a "dry joint"?
options: A joint cleaned with alcohol
A poor joint where solder did not bond
A joint made with no flux
A joint that was cooled down quickly with air

questions.stem: Why should soldering be done with fume extraction or good ventilation?
options: To keep the iron hot
To make the solder flow faster
To stop the board from bending
The fumes can harm your lungs

questions.stem: Which tool removes melted solder from a joint so that a part can be taken out?
options: A crimping tool for lugs and ferrules
A punch-down tool for data
A desoldering pump or braid
A cable stripper

questions.stem: Why is an anti-static wrist strap worn when handling some electronic parts?
options: Static from your body can damage the parts
It keeps your hands clean
It stops you from getting burnt by the iron
It holds the parts in place

questions.stem: Where should a hot soldering iron be placed when you are not using it?
options: On the bench beside the board
In your tool bag
On a piece of paper
In its stand

questions.stem: A fuse in a battery charger has blown. Why should you not fit a bigger fuse?
options: A bigger fuse will not fit the holder
It may not protect the charger from a fault
A bigger fuse will make the battery charge slower
A bigger fuse costs much more

questions.stem: A 12 V circuit draws 2 A. What is its resistance?
options: 6 Ω

questions.stem: In a 9 V battery circuit, how is the meter connected to measure the voltage across a resistor?
options: In parallel, across the resistor
In series, by breaking the circuit
Between the resistor and earth only
Across the battery with the leads swapped

questions.stem: How is a meter connected to measure the current in a battery circuit?
options: Across the battery terminals, side by side
In series, so the current flows through it
Across the resistor
Touching only one wire

questions.stem: What does a step-down transformer in a small power supply do?
options: Changes AC into smooth DC
Raises the voltage
Stores charge
Lowers the AC voltage

questions.stem: Which part changes AC into DC in a power supply?
options: The step-down transformer
The fuse
The rectifier (diodes)
The switch

questions.stem: The repair will cost more than a new appliance. What should you do?
options: Repair it anyway and send the customer the bill
Tell the customer and let them decide
Throw it away without asking
Keep it and sell the parts

questions.stem: What should be written on the repair record?
options: The fault found, parts used and test results
The customer's favourite colour
The time that the shop opened on that day and closed
Only the price of a brand new appliance

questions.stem: A repaired mains appliance has passed its dead tests. How is it first run at the Centre?
options: Plugged into any socket by the trainee who fixed it
Plugged in while the case is open
Run at home by the customer first
On a protected test bench by the instructor

questions.stem: A customer says her hair dryer smelt of burning before it stopped. What is a likely fault?
options: The cord is too long
The plug is the wrong colour
The motor or heater has overheated
The fan is turning too slowly to see

questions.stem: A table lamp works only when its cord is moved. What is the likely fault?
options: The lamp itself has blown
A broken or loose conductor
The wrong wattage of lamp is fitted
The lampshade is dirty and dusty

questions.stem: After fitting a new cord to an appliance, what stops the conductors being pulled off the terminals?
options: The cord grip, clamped on the outer sheath
A knot tied in the cord inside the plug
Insulating tape wound round the conductors
Glue on the terminals

questions.stem: What should you do with old circuit boards and batteries after a repair?
options: Burn them in the yard
Put them in the general rubbish bin
Put them in the e-waste collection
Bury them in the garden

questions.stem: An LED in a circuit does not light. Tests show it is fitted backwards. Why does that stop it working?
options: LEDs need AC to light up
The resistor in series blows when it is reversed
LEDs only work in the dark
An LED conducts in one direction only

questions.stem: Before you connect a 9 V battery to a repaired circuit, what should you check?
options: The battery is warm
The battery polarity matches the circuit
The battery is the largest size the shop sells
The battery has been used before

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

essays.stem: Describe a step-by-step method for finding the fault in an appliance that has stopped working.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would collect information: I would ask the customer what the appliance does or does not do, when the fault started, and whether there was a smell, a bang or a drop. Next I would make it safe by unplugging it and keeping the plug in view. Then I would inspect it by eye, outside and inside: the cord, plug, case, switch and terminals, looking for damage, burn marks, loose wires or signs of water. Next I would test with the power off, using a multimeter on the ohms range to check the cord, switch, fuses, thermostat and the main part, such as the element or motor winding. I would use the half-split method: test at the middle of the circuit, then in the half where the fault is, until the faulty part is found. I would then find out why it failed. Finally I would repair it with a correct part, test it again and record the work.
markingPoints: Collects information from the customer about the fault
Makes it safe by unplugging and keeping the plug in view
Inspects by eye for damage, burning, loose wires or water
Tests with the power off, in a logical order such as the half-split method
Finds the cause, repairs with a correct part, retests and records

essays.stem: Explain the safety precautions you would follow when troubleshooting and repairing electrical and electronic apparatus.
essays.modelAnswer: Before opening any mains appliance, I would unplug it and keep the plug where I can see it, so nobody can plug it in. For equipment that is wired in, I would isolate it, lock off, tag and prove it dead with a voltage tester checked on a known live source before and after. I would never work on mains equipment while it is live. Large capacitors in power supplies can hold a charge after unplugging, so I would discharge them safely with a resistor tool, as the maker says. I would do my tests with the power off, using the ohms and continuity ranges. Any tests with power on are done only on extra-low-voltage battery circuits, or by the instructor on a protected test bench. I would use a soldering iron in its stand, with good ventilation, and wear safety glasses. I would use an anti-static strap for sensitive parts. I would keep the bench dry and tidy, and follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules.
markingPoints: Unplugs mains appliances and keeps the plug in view; isolates fixed equipment with lock, tag and prove dead
Never works on mains equipment live
Discharges large capacitors safely
Tests with power off; powered tests only on extra-low-voltage circuits or by the instructor on a protected bench
Safe soldering (stand, ventilation, eye protection), anti-static care, dry tidy bench

essays.stem: An electric kettle does not heat. Explain how you would find the fault using dead tests.
essays.modelAnswer: I would ask the customer what happened, then unplug the kettle and keep the plug in view. I would look at the cord, plug and base for damage, burns or water. With a multimeter on the ohms range, I would first test the cord: each conductor from the plug pin to its terminal in the base should show continuity. Then I would test the switch: it should show continuity when ON and none when OFF. Next I would test the thermostat or steam switch, and then the thermal fuse, which should both show continuity when cold. Then I would test the element: for an 1100 W element on 110 V the reading should be about 11 ohms; an open reading means it is broken. I would also test from the element terminals to the metal body: there should be no continuity, and an insulation resistance test should give a high reading. Whichever part fails is the fault. I would then look for why it failed, such as the kettle being switched on empty.
markingPoints: Asks the customer, unplugs and inspects by eye
Tests cord conductors end to end
Tests the switch ON and OFF, then the thermostat and thermal fuse
Tests the element against its expected resistance, about 11 ohms for 1100 W on 110 V
Checks element to body insulation and looks for the cause of the failure

essays.stem: Explain how to use a multimeter safely to measure resistance, voltage and current on a small battery-powered circuit.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would check the meter, its leads and its battery, and make sure the leads are in the right sockets for the test. To measure resistance, the circuit must have no power, so I would disconnect the battery. I would set the meter to the ohms range, touch the leads together to check for zero, then measure across the part, lifting one leg of the part from the board if other parts are in parallel with it. To measure voltage, I would reconnect the battery, set the meter to DC volts on a range above the battery voltage, and connect the leads in parallel, across the part, with red to the positive side. To measure current, I would switch off, move the red lead to the current socket, set the current range, break the circuit and connect the meter in series, then switch on. Afterwards I would move the red lead back to the voltage socket so the meter is not damaged next time.
markingPoints: Checks meter, leads and battery; leads in the correct sockets
Resistance: power off, ohms range, check zero, lift a leg if needed
Voltage: DC volts on a suitable range, connected in parallel, correct polarity
Current: lead to the current socket, meter in series, power off while connecting
Returns the lead to the voltage socket after measuring current

essays.stem: Describe how you would replace a damaged power cord on an appliance with a metal case, and how you would test it.
essays.modelAnswer: I would unplug the appliance and keep the plug in view. I would choose a new cord of the same type, size and current rating, with three conductors so the metal case can be earthed. I would open the appliance, note or photograph how the old cord was connected, and remove it. I would pass the new cord through the cord grip, strip the outer sheath just enough so that the grip will clamp on the sheath, and strip the conductors to the right length without nicking the strands. I would connect line, neutral and earth to the correct terminals, with the earth conductor a little longer so it would be the last to pull off. I would tighten the terminals and the cord grip. At the plug end I would fit the correct plug, wired the same way. Then I would test: earth continuity from the plug's earth pin to the metal case, insulation resistance between the live conductors and the case, and a visual check, before the instructor does a function test.
markingPoints: Unplugs; chooses a three-core cord of the right type and rating
Records the old connections and fits the cord through the cord grip on the sheath
Strips correctly and connects line, neutral and earth to the right terminals; earth slightly longer
Fits and wires the plug correctly; all terminals tight
Tests earth continuity and insulation resistance before a supervised function test

essays.stem: Describe how you would test a resistor, a diode, an LED and an electrolytic capacitor that you think may be faulty.
essays.modelAnswer: All these tests are done with the power off and any large capacitor discharged. For a resistor, I would read its value from the colour bands, lift one leg from the board, and measure it on the ohms range. The reading should be close to the marked value, within its tolerance; an open reading or a very different value means it is faulty, and burn marks are a clear sign. For a diode, I would use the meter's diode test. With red on the anode and black on the cathode it should show a reading, and with the leads reversed it should show no reading. A reading both ways means it is shorted, and no reading either way means it is open. An LED is tested the same way; on many meters it will glow faintly in the forward direction. For an electrolytic capacitor, I would look for bulging or leaking, which mean it must be replaced, and measure it with a capacitance range if the meter has one.
markingPoints: Power off and capacitors discharged first
Resistor: read bands, lift a leg, compare the reading with the marked value
Diode: diode test both ways, reading one way only; explains shorted and open results
LED: tested like a diode
Capacitor: look for bulging or leaking; measure capacitance if possible

essays.stem: Describe how to remove a faulty part from a circuit board and solder in a new one.
essays.modelAnswer: With the power off and any capacitors discharged, I would note which way round the old part is fitted, especially for diodes, LEDs and electrolytic capacitors. I would heat each joint with a clean, tinned soldering iron and remove the melted solder with a desoldering pump or braid, then gently lift the part out without damaging the copper tracks. I would clean the holes and pads. I would fit the new part of the same value and rating, the right way round, and bend the legs slightly to hold it. To solder, I would heat the pad and the leg together for a moment, then feed the solder onto the joint, not onto the iron, so it flows around the leg and pad. I would remove the solder, then the iron, and let it cool without moving. A good joint is smooth, shiny and cone-shaped. I would trim the legs, check for bridges between joints, and clean off any flux. The iron goes back in its stand.
markingPoints: Power off; notes the direction of polarised parts
Desolders with a pump or braid without damaging tracks; cleans the pads
Fits the correct new part the right way round
Heats pad and leg, feeds solder to the joint, leaves it to cool undisturbed
Checks for a shiny joint and no bridges; trims legs; iron back in its stand

essays.stem: Describe the checks and tests you would do on a repaired mains appliance before it is returned to the customer.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would make sure the appliance is fully reassembled, with all screws, covers and guards in place, no tools or loose parts inside and no damaged parts on the outside. I would check that the cord grip holds the cord sheath firmly and that the plug is sound and correctly wired. Then I would do the dead tests with the appliance unplugged. For an appliance with a metal case, I would test earth continuity from the plug's earth pin to the metal case; the reading should be low. I would then do an insulation resistance test between the live conductors, joined together at the plug, and the earth pin or metal case; the reading should be high. I would test that the switch and any thermostat work correctly by continuity. Only when all these tests pass would the appliance be given a function test, by the instructor or a competent person on a protected test bench. Finally I would record the results and fit a label showing it has been tested.
markingPoints: Fully reassembled with covers and guards, nothing loose inside
Cord grip and plug checked
Earth continuity from the plug earth pin to the metal case
Insulation resistance between live conductors and earth or case
Function test only after the dead tests pass, by a competent person on a protected bench; results recorded

essays.stem: Explain why it is important to find the cause of a fault, not just replace the part that failed. Give an example.
essays.modelAnswer: A part often fails because something else is wrong. If I only replace the failed part, the same fault may happen again soon, the customer will be unhappy, and the appliance may become dangerous. For example, a kettle's thermal fuse may blow because the thermostat or steam switch is faulty and does not switch the element off, or because the kettle is often switched on empty. If I fit a new thermal fuse without checking the thermostat, the kettle could overheat again, and the new fuse would blow. In another example, a fuse in a battery charger may blow because a diode in the rectifier is shorted. A new fuse would blow at once, or a bigger fuse could let the charger overheat and catch fire. So after finding the failed part, I would test the parts around it, look for signs such as burning or water, and ask the customer how it was used. I would explain the real cause to the customer and record it.
markingPoints: A failed part is often a result of another fault
Replacing only the part may lead to the same failure again or a dangerous fault
Gives a clear, correct example such as a thermal fuse and a faulty thermostat
Tests the parts around the failed part and asks how the item was used
Explains the cause to the customer and records it

essays.stem: Describe how you would deal with the customer and complete the paperwork for an appliance repair.
essays.modelAnswer: When the customer brings in the appliance, I would listen carefully and write down their name, contact number, the appliance, and the fault in their own words. I would give them a receipt or job number. After finding the fault, I would tell the customer what is wrong and what the repair will cost, and how long it will take. If the repair costs more than a new appliance, or the appliance is unsafe to repair, I would explain this and let them decide. I would not do extra work without their agreement. When the repair is done, I would complete the repair record: the fault found, the cause, the parts used, the time taken and the test results. When the customer collects it, I would explain in plain words what was done and how to use the appliance safely, and hand over any old parts if they ask for them. Finally I would clean the bench and put waste and e-waste in the right bins.
markingPoints: Records the customer's details and the fault in their words; gives a job number
Explains the fault, cost and time, and gets agreement before the work
Lets the customer decide when repair is not worth it or not safe
Completes the repair record with fault, cause, parts and test results
Explains the repair and safe use at handover; cleans up and sorts waste

practical1.title: Troubleshoot and repair a faulty mains appliance using dead tests
practical1.brief: The instructor gives the group a mains appliance with a metal case, such as an electric kettle or a table lamp, with one or two faults set on purpose, and a job card with the customer's description of the fault. The appliance stays unplugged for the whole task, with its plug in view on the bench. As a group, inspect it by eye, then use dead tests only to find the faults: continuity of the cord, switch, thermostat, thermal fuse and element or lampholder, and earth continuity to the case. Write each test and result on the job card. Repair the faults with the parts the instructor supplies, then test earth continuity and insulation resistance. The group does not plug the appliance in; any function test is done afterwards by the instructor on the Centre's protected test bench. Every member makes at least two tests, and each takes part in the repair. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group with the completed job card.
materials: A metal-cased mains appliance with set faults, and its job card
Replacement parts from the instructor (for example a cord, thermal fuse or lampholder)
Screwdrivers, wire strippers, side cutters, long-nose pliers
photos: The appliance unplugged on the bench, with the plug in view
The visual inspection, showing any damage found
A continuity test on the cord conductors, with the meter reading
The test that found each fault, with its reading
The repair being made with the new part
The earth continuity and insulation resistance readings after repair
The completed job card and repair record
checklist: Kept the appliance unplugged for the whole task
Carried out a careful visual inspection first
Used the multimeter on the right range for each dead test
Tested in a logical order and found the set faults
Repaired with the correct part, with the cord grip and terminals secure
Did the earth continuity and insulation resistance tests after repair
Recorded tests, faults, causes and parts clearly
Left the bench clean and returned tools and meters
safety: The appliance is never plugged in by the group; any function test is done by the instructor on the protected test bench
Warn others before an insulation resistance test and keep hands clear during it
Wear safety glasses when cutting and stripping wires
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules

practical2.title: Find and repair faults on a battery-powered LED circuit board
practical2.brief: The instructor gives the group a small circuit board that runs from a 9 V battery, with LEDs, resistors, a diode and a capacitor, and two or three faults set on purpose (for example a dry joint, an LED fitted backwards, or a wrong resistor). No mains supply is used in this task. With the battery disconnected, inspect the board by eye, then test the parts with the multimeter: resistor values, diode and LED direction, and track continuity. Find each fault and repair it by desoldering and resoldering the part. Then connect the 9 V battery the right way round and measure the voltage across the battery and across each LED. Write every test and result on the job sheet. Every member makes at least two meter tests and makes at least one soldered joint while the assessor watches. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group with the job sheet.
materials: Circuit board with set faults and a 9 V battery with clip
Spare resistors, LEDs and a diode of the right values
Soldering iron with stand, solder, desoldering pump or braid
Safety glasses and fume extraction or a well-ventilated bench
photos: The board with the battery disconnected, before testing
A resistor being measured with one leg lifted, showing the reading
The diode or LED test, showing the result both ways
A new soldered joint, close up, showing a smooth shiny finish
The board working on the 9 V battery, with a voltage being measured
The completed job sheet, and the bench cleaned
checklist: Kept the battery disconnected while testing resistance and soldering
Read resistor values and measured them correctly
Tested diodes and LEDs both ways and judged the result correctly
Found the set faults by logical testing
Desoldered without lifting the tracks and fitted parts the right way round
Made smooth, shiny joints with no bridges
Connected the battery with the right polarity and measured voltage in parallel
Kept the iron in its stand, recorded results and left the bench clean
safety: No mains supply is used in this task; the board runs only from a 9 V battery
Keep the soldering iron in its stand when not in use; the tip is very hot
Wear safety glasses when soldering and trimming legs
Use fume extraction or work in a well-ventilated place; wash hands after soldering
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
